Adult Bali sardinella (Sardinella lemuru) attain a maximum total length of 23 cm [Li = 23 cm], which positions this species among the medium-sized members of the genus Sardinella within the family Dorosomatidae. Length-frequency distributions from purse-seine landings off the coast of Bali indicate that individuals approach this asymptotic size gradually over several years, though the growth rate slows considerably after the onset of maturity. The length-mass relationship, derived from morphometric measurements of commercially sampled specimens, follows the equation W = 0.00741 × L³·⁰⁹, a scaling exponent typical of small coastal clupeiforms. Using this relationship, the calculated ultimate wet weight at the asymptotic length reaches 119.6 grams [Wwi = 119.6 grams], a value that aligns well with published records for similarly sized tropical sardines. This body mass confers a degree of resilience against gape-limited predators, though the species remains a critical prey item for larger pelagic fishes like tuna and mackerel throughout its range in the eastern Indian Ocean and adjacent seas of Southeast Asia.

Puberty in Sardinella lemuru is attained at a total length of 14.3 cm [Lp = 14.3 cm], a threshold that corresponds to approximately 62 percent of the ultimate length and marks the transition from a predominantly somatic to a mixed somatic-reproductive growth trajectory. The corresponding wet weight at this developmental milestone, calculated from the length-mass relationship, is 27.5 grams [Wwp = 27.5 grams]. Histological examination of gonadal tissue from specimens collected in the Lombok Strait reveals that vitellogenesis and spermatogenesis become active once individuals exceed this size, with peak reproductive activity coinciding with the monsoon-driven upwelling season that enhances local phytoplankton productivity. The relatively early onset of maturity compared to some temperate congeners likely reflects the selective pressures of a high-mortality, low-latitude environment where early breeding confers a clear fitness advantage despite the trade-off with somatic growth.

At a stable water temperature of 27.8 °C [T = 27.8 °C], which approximates the mean annual sea surface temperature across the species core habitat in the Bali Strait, embryonic development proceeds rapidly. The incubation period from fertilization to hatching is just 4 days [ab = 4 days], a short duration that reduces the window of vulnerability for the demersal, adhesive eggs to benthic predators and physical disturbance at a temperature of 27.8 °C [T = 27.8 °C]. The newly hatched yolk-sac larva emerges at a wet weight of 0.00018 grams [Wwb = 0.00018 grams], a mass consistent with the small egg diameter of 0.7 millimeters measured from gravid females captured during spawning surveys. This minute size, while energetically economical for the female to produce in large numbers, imposes a narrow window for the onset of exogenous feeding, as the endogenous yolk reserves are exhausted within roughly 48 hours post-eclosion under the same thermal regime.

When maintained at 27.8 °C [T = 27.8 °C], sexually mature females exhibit a maximum reproductive output of approximately 70 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 70 eggs per day], with this peak rate typically observed during the height of the spawning season between August and October. Batch spawning over an extended period allows females to spread reproductive risk across temporal variation in larval food availability, a common adaptation among small pelagic fishes inhabiting dynamic upwelling ecosystems.

Comparisons with congeneric species such as Sardinella gibbosa and Sardinella longiceps reveal that the maximum length of 23 cm [Li = 23 cm] in Bali sardinella is intermediate between those taxa, which reach 20 and 24 centimeters, respectively. The wet weight at birth of 0.00018 grams [Wwb = 0.00018 grams] is typical among tropical clupeiforms with pelagic larval stages, reflecting a conserved constraint on egg size imposed by the trade-off between fecundity and per-offspring investment. Field surveys conducted across multiple years indicate that the species total length at puberty of 14.3 cm [Lp = 14.3 cm] is remarkably stable across populations, suggesting strong canalization of this life-history trait despite regional variation in water temperature and food availability. The calculated wet weight at puberty of 27.5 grams [Wwp = 27.5 grams] at this size further highlights the tight coupling between somatic growth and reproductive development in this commercially important small pelagic fish.
